claims.text: Adding approximately 3–5 atomic percent copper during alloy synthesis will promote the formation of nanoscale, uniformly distributed copper precipitates.
Uniformly dispersed nanoscale copper precipitates can enhance thermal-conduction pathways in the high-entropy alloy.
Uniformly dispersed nanoscale copper precipitates can preserve the overall microstructural stability of the alloy.
Copper has intrinsically high thermal conductivity.
A nanoscale copper dispersion creates conductive channels within the high-entropy-alloy matrix.
If the copper phase does not coarsen or segregate, it will minimally disrupt dislocation motion.
If the copper phase does not coarsen or segregate, it will minimally disrupt grain-boundary cohesion.
Adding 3–5 atomic percent copper is expected to increase effective thermal conductivity by approximately 10–15% relative to the copper-free baseline alloy.
The copper-modified alloy is expected to maintain yield strength within acceptable limits for reactor application.
The copper-modified alloy is expected to maintain toughness within acceptable limits for reactor application.
The expected improvement should hold at approximately 600–750 °C under mechanical loading representative of plasma-facing intermediate-layer service.
The current copper-free intermediate-layer high-entropy alloy has lower thermal conductivity than the proposed copper-modified alloy.
The current copper-free intermediate-layer high-entropy alloy has established structural robustness.
Copper coarsening or phase segregation caused by excessive copper could compromise the alloy's mechanical properties.
